Sources disagree. One party found a 30 m rope 'more than enough' for a single rappel to the ledge; another party with a 30 m rope needed an intermediate anchor and two rappels; a third used a 60 m rope and still found it did not reach the next anchor, building extra anchors; a fourth made several double- and single-rope rappels. results.correct_value: 8,300 ft gain and loss (5,000 ft landing to basin camp + 3,300 ft summit day).
results.evidence: 7,248 ft is exactly the summit (8,348 ft) minus lake level (~1,100 ft) — net relief, a floor that the undulating river trail and the descending traverse around the cliff bands into the east basin must exceed. The itinerary's three days (5,000 + 3,300 gain; 3,300 + 5,000 loss) and its totalNote ('8,000+ ft') agree, and a measured trip report of this exact plan gives ~10 mi/5,000 ft to the 5,400 ft camp and 3,300 ft for the summit day. A second report gives the trip's elevation range as 1,160-8,360 ft, consistent with 7,248 being net relief only.

results.correct_value: Bird Creek Camp is in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (national forest), beyond the NRA; no North Cascades backcountry permit is needed for a night there.

patches.find: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping.
patches.replace: The camp lies in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, a few miles above where the Devore Creek trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so no North Cascades backcountry permit is needed for a night here; that permit applies only to a night at a camp inside the recreation area, such as Weaver Point.
